body: The last morning of summer, and Marisol is showing off. At twelve past seven the light comes into 412 low and level off the Lagoon, which lies out there flat as a plate, not a ripple on it, and the window is cracked its two inches on the Grove, so the room smells of eucalyptus with nothing to damp it down: menthol, dust, a little cat. No fog all week, says the forecast on Theo’s phone.

Two cards are lying on the carpet inside the door where somebody slid them under it in the night. Black borders. Heavy stock. The borders were ruled by hand and cut with scissors by someone who believes in doing a thing properly and doesn’t own a paper cutter, and not one corner of either card is square. Jack picks up the one with his name on it.

The iPhone is lit under the sheet; he reads everything about Jack before Jack does, on principle, and he has already been through her photos. “Friday,” he says, “you have a date with the cattle baroness.” “She can butcher a deer.” The sheet comes down. Theo turns his head on the pillow, all the way, slowly, to look at him. “Say that again. Slower. I want to remember where I was.” “She told me at the cleanup. She’s pulled a calf.” Theo lies back with the iPhone on his chest, enchanted, already casting it. Then, lightly, still scrolling: “You told me you weren’t doing anything. I believed you.” A sigh, with some craft in it. “I’m a very trusting person.”

body: Twelve-ten on a Tuesday at St. Brendan’s is twenty people and a great deal of boat. The ceiling goes up over them in its long overturned hull, and the noon light comes down through the blue glass and lies across the pews in panels the color of a swimming pool after dark. Green on the altar, green on the priest: Ordinary Time, the long green middle of the year. Mrs. Fitch in her pew by the shrine with her purse squared on her knees. The old man with the cane, who takes the aisle seat and always will. Two rows up, Becca Lindell, braid down her back to the belt, a rosary wound twice around her wrist; a 12:10 regular, it turns out, in between labs. And Kevin in his navy quarter-zip, who has saved Jack a seat with a Bible open on it to the day’s Gospel.

Lena comes in during the opening prayer. Bare-headed, no lace today, the oatmeal cardigan over a green dress, and she slides into the pew on Jack’s other side without a word or a look, genuflecting so fast it’s mostly knee, and folds her hands in her lap like she has been there since the bell.

Osei is saying the whole Mass himself, as he said he would. He reads the Gospel too. Luke, eight: Jesus in a house so full that his own family can’t get through the door, and somebody has to pass the message over the heads of the crowd. *Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, and they wish to see you.* “My mother and my brothers,” Osei reads, “are those who hear the word of God and act on it.”
Jack hears *brothers*.

Osei doesn’t go to the ambo to preach. He stands where he read, takes the reading glasses off their cord, and says two sentences to the twenty of them. “They could not get in for the crowd. He does not send them away — he makes the room bigger.” Then he goes to his chair and sits, and the church is quiet enough to hear the old man’s cane slide along the pew.

At the prayers of the faithful he reads the intentions off an index card in his own hand: the sick, the dead, the President. And last, without lifting his eyes from the card: “For the intention of Carmela Rinaldi, in thanksgiving.” He gives it nothing else. No grandmother, no grandson, no reason. Lena was right there a week ago Sunday when Mrs. Fitch read the whole slip out loud, *good confession* and all. She keeps her eyes on the altar. The corner of her mouth tucks in, very slightly, until the Our Father.

After the blessing Kevin squeezes Jack’s shoulder, mouths *orgo* with tragic eyebrows, and is gone up the aisle at a jog. Osei catches Jack in the vestibule, still in the green, and hands him an envelope.

body: “A grandmother likes paper,” Osei says. “Mail it today. At her age a letter is a house call.” “Thank you, Father.” “*Me da wo ase* is the correct reply,” Osei says, delighted with him, “but you will get there,” and limps off toward the sacristy.

Lena is at the Marian shrine with a dollar in the box and a taper, lighting one candle low on the rack. When she comes back up the side aisle she says, “For Carmela,” as if he’d asked. Then, lower, walking out: “Did you tell him I said he’s welcome?” “Mailed it yesterday.” She nods once. “Did she ask you twice again?” “Haven’t called.” “Call.”

Becca is waiting outside the door in the full sun, Wranglers and a Carhartt vest and a spiral planner under her arm, and she doesn’t bother with hello. “Friday. Six. I’ll drive. I have a truck.” She holds up a key ring on a steel carabiner. “My brother Eli’s. A Ranger.” She beams past him. “Hi, Lena!” And she’s off across the courtyard at a ranch walk, late for a lab, the braid swinging.

Lena watches her all the way to Ocean Road. “She has a truck.” “Her brother’s. A Ranger.” “Of course she has a truck.” It sounds like admiration. Then she turns and looks at him, and it’s the lifeguard tower again, Sunday, the same instruction, shorter: “Find out what you’re doing.”

Before he can do anything with that she has a black-bordered card out of her cardigan pocket, its corners as crooked as his. “Mine says bring the other Catholic.” “That’s me.” “Yours says it too?” “Bring the other Catholic.” She looks at the card, at the olive tree, at him. “Then we’re each other’s plus-one.”

body: Half-price chowder Tuesday is down to its last pot and its last four customers, and for the first time since seven the dish pit has caught up with itself. The Hobart lets out its steam on the cycle and the steam goes up into the light over the pass and hangs there. Somebody has put a quarter in the jukebox for Patsy Cline, “Walkin’ After Midnight,” which at twenty to twelve is a little on the nose, and Gloria gives the jukebox a look on her way by with the pot. Over the register the chalkboard says PIE OF THE DAY: PECAN in her capitals, and on the board beside it, the one she put up for him his first week, JACK’S RATINGS: MARIONBERRY 4/10 · OLALLIEBERRY 9/10.

On the far stool by the kitchen, Ray Ochoa is eating the meatloaf. Tuesdays, meatloaf, black coffee: Jack had him placed by the second sentence on Ocean Road, badge wallet open, and here he is in the navy windbreaker. When the plate came up in the window he lifted his chin at Rudy, and Rudy, behind the heat lamps, lifted his back, and that was the whole conversation; from the ease of it, it’s been going on for years. Ray eats like there’s a clock somewhere only he can see. At 11:52 he leaves a ten under the saucer and zips the windbreaker, and passing the end of the pass, without turning his head: “Light working, Mr. Costigan?” “Yes, sir.” “Good.” The bell over the door. The gray Crown Vic backs out under the wharf lamp and is gone up Mission.

At midnight Jack asks Gloria if she’ll sell him a whole pie. “For what?” “A funeral.” Gloria sets the pot on the warmer. “Whose?” “A cigarette’s.” At the flattop Rudy, back to both of them, who has been listening to every word the way he listens to Vin Scully, crosses himself with the spatula hand and goes on scraping.

Gloria wants all of it: whose cigarette, who’s burying it, and who the pie is *for*. Jack does his best. All black, he says. From Portland. No body temperature anybody has ever measured. Keeps a whiteboard in the fourth-floor lounge with his name on it and a running score. Says he upholds the patriarchy. “Do you?” “I wash dishes, Gloria.” She closes her eyes, the pencil in the gray bun, and rates her sight unseen. “Rhubarb. Tart, and nobody can decide if it’s a fruit.” “It’s a vegetable.” “It’s a vegetable, hon. That’s the point.” She has rhubarb in the freezer since June and one pie baked off it sitting in the case, untouched. “Nobody’s complained,” Gloria says. “Nobody orders it.”
“Who else is going?” “The other Catholic.” Gloria looks at him over the pot, the look she gave the jukebox. She doesn’t ask which.

A whole pie is sixteen dollars. She writes eight on the ticket and underlines it twice. “Bereavement discount.” He pays it out of tonight’s tips, which come to eleven dollars and a Canadian quarter, and she takes the eight and slides the quarter back across the Formica, because it’s Canadian. Then she puts her hand on top of the pie case. “So. Which.”

journal.text: Marionberry: 4/10. Olallieberry: 9/10 — Dad would eat two pieces and complain about the second. Gloria rated Lena: pecan. s05.slug: WEDNESDAY · 1:35 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE ROOF
s05.music: The Smiths — “There Is a Light That Never Goes Out”
body: At the east end of the fifth floor, past the last door and the smell of somebody’s microwave popcorn, the stairs go up one more half-flight to a steel door painted institutional beige. Red on white, at eye level: EMERGENCY EXIT ONLY · ALARM WILL SOUND. Under it, in Sharpie gone brown, in a small and patient hand: *(it won’t)*. A popsicle stick, gray from a decade of thumbs, is wedged in the strike plate.

body.text: The widow is asking after her pie. I told her you were detained at the border.

body: Jack has the Anchor’s white pie box flat on one palm and the rest of him smells like the Hobart: steam, bleach, the last of the chowder in the cuffs of his flannel. He puts his hip to the bar and braces for the whole building: three hundred and ten freshmen on the lawn in towels, Priya’s air horn. The door swings out onto the night. Nothing happens. Nothing at all.

Tar and gravel shift under his work shoes. The elevator housing stands up in the middle of the roof like a little concrete chapel, two HVAC boxes hum, and a parapet runs around the edge at hip height. The Lagoon lies flat and black one way with the Anacapa lights laid in it; the hills are a darker black the other way, with the stars starting right where they stop. No moon. Clear and dry and cold enough to want the flannel. There are more stars over Marisol than Youngstown has had even since the mills went and took the smoke with them.

Margot presides. All black, the oxblood Docs, a Mason jar on the gravel with a candle burning low inside it, and beside it an oxblood Doc Martens shoebox with the lid off: the casket. One pack of Djarum Black lies inside on a fold of black tissue paper. On a cooler: a magnum of Charles Shaw, a sleeve of plastic cups, and a white iPod dock the size of a toaster, out of which the Smiths are playing just loud enough not to reach the fifth floor.

Lena is cross-legged on a Saints beach towel, black and gold with a fleur-de-lis the size of a hubcap, in the oatmeal cardigan and the boots, a plastic cup of red resting on her knee. Laney is asleep in a folding lawn chair under Margot’s black peacoat, a pink Pi Lam bandana tied over her hair and one Tory Burch flat lying on the gravel where it fell. Pledge line-up ran till midnight, Lena says, and she made it up the stairs on spite. Theo is on top of the elevator housing with the 5D at his eye, in a black tuxedo jacket over a T-shirt — black tie optional; he opted for half — filming the wake from the high ground. All night he never comes within a body’s length of the parapet. Kevin sits against the near HVAC box with a steel thermos, in a plain gray T-shirt.
“I’m here in a medical capacity,” Kevin says, and lifts the thermos. “Somebody at a funeral for a cigarette should know CPR.”
“Costigan,” Theo calls down. “Don’t look at the lens. Look at the casket.”
Margot doesn’t look at her watch. “You’re late,” she says. “Lena said one o’clock. I allowed for the bicycle. I didn’t allow for the pie.”
Jack sets the box on the cooler and opens it.

body.text: Margot leans over it with her hands clasped behind her back. Deep purple, the lattice gone dark at the edges, the juice already through the bottom of the box. “This is the good pie?” “It’s a nine,” Jack says. Margot straightens. “From you,” she says, “that’s a sonnet.”

Lena is up on her knees before Margot can get to it. She takes the plastic knife out of the sleeve, cuts the first slice without asking anybody, and looks at it on the paper plate — the dark top, the glaze, the pecans laid in rings. “Pecan,” she says. Then she looks at Jack, once. “Sweet all the way through. I’ve been told.” Margot looks from one of them to the other, decides not to ask, and takes the second slice.

Margot looks at the pink, sour-smelling inside of it. “Rhubarb is a vegetable,” she says. “Gloria says that’s the point,” Jack says. Margot opens her mouth to ask who Gloria is and doesn’t. She cuts a slice, very straight, and holds the paper plate on her flat palm and says nothing at all, and Lena, watching her, smiles at her knees.

body: Margot pours him a cup of Charles Shaw, the house red of the bereaved, and Jack takes it and decides it’s going to last him all night. Lena shifts over on the towel and gives him the end with the fleur-de-lis on it.

In the lawn chair Laney sighs and turns her face into the peacoat collar. Lena reaches over without getting up. She lifts the edge of the coat, slides her hand into the pocket of Laney’s pink cardigan, and takes out the little silver pillbox with DRP on the lid. She opens it with her thumbnail. She counts with one finger, touching each pill. She closes it, puts it back, and smooths the coat down over Laney’s shoulder. Then she looks up, and Jack is watching her. She looks back at him, level, for as long as it takes him to understand there’s no explanation coming. Then she picks up her wine, and the Smiths keep going on the cooler.

Margot stands over him with a fresh pack, the black paper and the gold band, the cellophane already off. The smell comes up out of the pack like a spice cabinet on fire. She holds one out to him, filter first. “It’s a wake,” she says. “Everybody takes one.”

journal.title: The roof
journal.text: Fifth floor: EMERGENCY EXIT ONLY · ALARM WILL SOUND, and under it, in Sharpie gone brown: (it won’t). It doesn’t. A popsicle stick in the strike. Tar, gravel, the elevator housing, a parapet to the hip. The Lagoon one way, the hills the other.

choices.key: On the roof Lena took a clove out of your mouth. Reliquary No. 4 — by dispensation.
response: Margot holds the lighter for him herself. The clove catches and crackles like a fire in a wet log, little snaps all along the paper, and the smoke is sweet, sweeter than it has any right to be, and goes straight to the back of his head on top of the wine.

He gets two drags. On the third Lena leans across the fleur-de-lis, takes it out of his mouth by the filter, and holds it up to the candle. There follows a theological pause. Then she pinches it out against the Mason jar, digs the Altoids tin out of her cardigan pocket, tears a strip off the bottom of her own funeral card and writes on it against her knee with Margot’s pen: *No. 4 · 9/23/09 · the Delgado roof · a clove, by dispensation.* The slip goes in. The lid goes on.
“That’s desecration,” Margot says.
“That’s *veneration*,” says Lena, and puts the tin back in her pocket.

journal.title: The Reliquary
journal.text: An Altoids tin from a pea-soup restaurant in Buellton. RELIQUARY on the lid. No. 1: the Lighthouse. No. 2: Malibu, before breakfast. No. 3: the harbor — she smoked half of it first. No. 4: a clove, on the Delgado roof, at a wake. By dispensation. Do not ask.

choices.text: Hold it, unlit, for the length of the service.
response: He takes it and doesn’t ask for the lighter. He holds it upright between finger and thumb, filter down, like a taper at the Easter Vigil at St. Brigid’s the year he was nine and terrified of setting Mrs. Iannucci’s hair on fire.
Margot looks at it, and at him. “Correct,” she says, and goes back to the candle.
Margot draws the clove back and returns it to the pack with exaggerated care, and keeps the pack in her hand where he can see it. “Puritan,” she says.
On the towel Lena leans back on her hands and looks up at the stars as if somebody had just told her a secret about them.

s05b.slug: WEDNESDAY · 1:46 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE ROOF
body: The song ends. Margot doesn’t touch the iPod. The silence comes in after it — the hum of the HVAC, a car out on Ocean Road, the eucalyptus in the Grove ticking in the breeze — and keeps coming until it has become part of the service. Then she stands up by the candle with an index card in her hand. She never once looks at it.
“Dearly beloved. We are gathered here today to bury a cigarette.”
Up on the elevator housing the 5D’s little red light is on.

“She was born in Kudus, in Central Java, in 1951, to a family firm called Djarum, which means *needle*. She came to Portland by way of a head shop on Hawthorne Boulevard, where a man named Dez sold her to me at sixteen with no questions asked — the only liberty I have ever been offered without a reading list.”
Lena makes a small sound into her wine. Margot waits for it to finish.
“She crackled. People assume that’s a metaphor. It’s eugenol — clove oil — boiling in the shreds. She was the only thing I owned that announced herself.
“She was sweet. She was bad for me. She was *mine*.

“On the twenty-second of June the President signed the Family Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act, and as of today she is contraband. The Commissioner of Food and Drugs explained that flavored cigarettes are a gateway for children. I was a child. I went through the gateway. On the other side was a roof. You may assess the outcome.”
Kevin, against the HVAC box, raises his thermos an inch, to the outcome.

“Strawberry is dead. Chocolate is dead. Vanilla, cinnamon, clove: dead. Menthol was spared. Which is to say the cigarette Black America was sold for fifty years was spared, because Congress knows who has a lobby and who has a funeral.”

Nobody on the roof moves for that one. Jack has been to a lot of funerals — the South Side of Youngstown buries somebody every Saturday and feeds everybody after — and he has heard monsignors say less in twenty minutes.
“It’s Padre Pio’s day,” Lena says from the towel, quietly — it’s after midnight, so it is. “He took snuff, they say. You’d have gotten along.”

Margot doesn’t break stride. “Put him in the program.” She turns the index card over, which is the only thing she does with it. “She is survived by a carton in my closet, which I will smoke at the rate of one per grief, and by the Djarum Black cigarillo, a legal loophole I consider unworthy of her.”

“From the Book of Common Prayer,” she says. “Burial at sea. I chose it for the prose.” She kneels on the gravel. She takes the last pack out of its tissue paper, slides one cigarette out, lays it alone in the shoebox, and puts the lid on. Her hand stays flat on the lid while she says the rest of it, and her voice doesn’t change at all.
“We therefore commit this body to the deep, to be turned into corruption.” On the towel Lena crosses herself, small and quick, and Margot lets her.
Up on the housing, Theo lowers the camera. He doesn’t raise it again.
Margot stops. The candle leans in the jar and straightens. “The rest of the sentence is for believers,” she says. “I’m told it’s beautiful.”

She stands and brushes the gravel off her knees. Then, to the roof at large, in the same voice she used for the strawberries: “Today the state decided what I may put into my own body. It will not be the last time.”
Lena sets her cup down on the towel very slowly. “Oh, Margot,” she says. “You did *not*.”

In the lawn chair Laney opens her eyes. She takes in the candle, the shoebox, Margot standing over it in black, and her face crumples all at once, like a pageant runner-up’s, magnificently. “It’s so *sad*,” she sobs, and starts to applaud — big, slow, Miss-Congeniality applause — and is asleep again before her hands have finished the second clap. They come to rest on the peacoat, a few inches apart, mid-applause.

Theo comes down off the elevator housing by the steel ladder on the far side, one-handed, the camera held up and away from the rungs. “She needs her bed,” he says. He holds the 5D out to Kevin. Kevin takes it by the strap and holds it away from his body, at the end of his arm.

Theo slides his arms under Laney and lifts her out of the lawn chair and out from under the peacoat, which stays behind on the chair in the shape of her. The bandana comes loose. She gets a fistful of his tuxedo lapel without waking up. “Theodore,” she says, into it.
“Delaney.”
Lena is half up off the towel. “On her side — ”
“I know,” Theo says.

Kevin steps in and hangs the camera around Theo’s neck by the strap, settling it against Laney’s shoulder, and steps back without a word. Jack picks up the Tory Burch flat off the gravel and lays it on Laney’s stomach. Then Theo carries her through the propped door and down, and it is ten after two, and there are four of them on the roof.

s06.slug: WEDNESDAY · 2:20 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE ROOF
body: Margot, Lena, Kevin, Jack. The candle in its jar, the magnum two-thirds down, what’s left of the pie in its tin on the cooler. Margot has not sat down since the committal, and it starts the way these things start, as sport — the two best arguers in Delgado who aren’t Jack, a bottle of Two-Buck Chuck, nowhere to be until one o’clock this afternoon, which doesn’t feel like the same day. Margot’s last line at the service was the opening bell, and both of them heard it ring.
“I’m serious,” Margot says. “If the state can take my cloves for my own good, it can take anything for my own good. You people should be terrified. You’re next.”
“Cher, we’ve been next since Nero,” Lena says. “It’s practically a liturgical season.”

Margot gives her that much with one nod and goes straight past it. Judith Jarvis Thomson, 1971: you wake up in a hospital bed, back to back with a famous violinist who is unconscious, and the Society of Music Lovers has plugged his kidneys into yours because you alone have the right blood type. Nine months, and he’ll recover. Unplug, and he dies. “Are you obliged to stay plugged in?”
“I’d stay,” Lena says. “And then I’d sue the Society of Music Lovers for kidnapping. It’s a beautiful argument, Margot, for a world where babies get in by burglary.”
“And when it *is* burglary?”

Lena doesn’t answer fast. Her thumb goes around the rim of the cup once. “Then it’s the hardest case there is,” she says. “And the child still didn’t break in.” Margot drinks, and the argument moves on.

Lena comes back with Don Marquis, 1989, and she says it like something she’s known by heart since she was fourteen. “What makes it wrong to kill you or me isn’t that we’re clever. It’s that it takes everything we were going to have. A baby has more future than anybody on this roof.” A flick of the wrist. “John Paul says the same thing with more Latin.”

“Then let’s talk about who pays for the future.” Margot counts it off on her fingers without hurrying, the candlelight going up the lenses of her glasses. “The woman. Nine months, a body that doesn’t go back, the job she loses, a state that won’t fund the crib, a Church that won’t hand out a condom, and men who legislate and leave.”
“Yes,” Lena says. “All of it but the condom, and I’ll fight you on that one sober.”

Margot waits for the rest of the *but*. It doesn’t come. Lena has given her everything else on the list, and she leans forward on the towel. “So the answer is a house. A room and a crib and somebody to drive you to the checkup. The Catholic Worker had that answer before anybody had a sign. I’m a pro-life Democrat, Margot. Both parties will sell that girl. One before the election and one after.”
“Your Dorothy Day had one,” Margot says. “Before she was Dorothy Day.”

“And spent the rest of her life on the other side of it.” Lena is going faster now, the drawl coming up under the words. “When a girl decides to keep it, everybody has an opinion and nobody has a crib.” Her hand is at the medal before the words are out — the small gold oval at her collarbone, her thumb over it — and holds it while she looks at Margot, and then she takes it away and picks up her wine.
Margot tops off her own cup. “And when we’re done with this, we’re doing Ephesians.”
“Not tonight,” say Jack and Lena, together.
“You can’t just say that.”
“We can,” Lena says. “It’s a liturgical response.”

Kevin has been quiet so long that when he talks the other three turn to look at him. He has the thermos cap in his hand and he’s turning it. “Trời sinh voi, trời sinh cỏ,” he says. “My Bà Nội says it. Every time somebody at church is pregnant again. Heaven makes the elephant, heaven makes the grass.” He screws the cap down. “Like — if God sends the kid, God sends what the kid eats.”
Margot considers him with real interest. “That’s beautiful,” she says, “and it isn’t an argument.”
“I know,” Kevin says, and smiles at her, the big one.

“Grass doesn’t feel anything,” Margot says, turning back to Lena. “Neither does a fetus at ten weeks. There’s nobody home yet. You can’t take a future from nobody.” And then, because he’s been sitting there on the end of the towel with the same cup of wine for forty minutes: “Costigan. You’ve been nursing that cup like it’s going to be taken up in the second collection. Contribute.”

choices.text: Press her: “Then what makes killing anybody wrong? Not that they’re awake. People sleep.”
response: He says it, and adds that Doug Pruitt sleeps fourteen hours a day and nobody’s ever tried to unplug him. Kevin, who lives with Doug Pruitt, raises the thermos in agreement.

Margot is ready for it. “A sleeper has somebody to wake up,” she says. “You’re describing someone who’s never been home.” But he can see it land a little anyway, and she doesn’t pretend it didn’t. “Fine. Then you’ll be wanting to fund the future, Costigan. Every crib. I’ll send you the bill.”
He holds the cup up to the candle so the light comes through it, thin and purple. “This,” he says, “is an argument for natural law. Something in here is clearly being violated.”

Margot makes a sound. She gets the plastic cup to her mouth in time to put most of it in there, and holds it there, and glares at him over the rim with genuine hatred while her shoulders go. Lena doesn’t bother hiding anything; she tips over sideways on the towel and laughs at the stars. “Charles Shaw,” she says when she can, “Doctor of the Church.”
Margot looks at him long enough that he can’t tell whether he’s about to be insulted or thanked.
“My mother thinks I should have been a Classicist,” she says. “On this she agrees with Lena.” And she turns back to the argument, and the argument closes over the question.

choices.text: Stay out of it. Keep the candle lit.
response: “Abstaining,” Jack says, and reaches over and cups his hand around the mouth of the Mason jar, where a breeze off the Lagoon has started to lay the flame down flat. It stands back up.
Kevin leans across the gravel and puts the thermos in his free hand, unprompted. The tea is hot and so sweet it makes his back teeth ache. “Bà Nội’s recipe,” Kevin says. “Too much sugar. On purpose.”

s06a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:02 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE ROOF
body: Forty minutes later the magnum is down to the label, Orion has come up sideways over the hills the way he does in the fall, and Lena has pushed the sleeves of the oatmeal cardigan up past her elbows. Jack has watched her do that in Hollis 302 since the first week. It means she’s about to win.

She reaches for the strongest thing she has. “You want to talk about who pays? Look at who doesn’t get to. Nine in ten, Margot. When the test comes back with an extra chromosome, nine in ten of them never get born. Somebody decided who gets counted, and it was a lab.”

Margot doesn’t move. No pen, no clove, no comeback — and Margot has had a comeback for everything since the first week of school, including the fire alarm. She sits with her cup in her lap and her eyes on the candle and her face doesn’t do anything at all.
Against the HVAC box, Kevin sets his thermos down on the gravel. Carefully, so it won’t make a sound.
Jack sees it a half second before Lena does. Lena has already taken the breath to go on.

choices.key: Mid-argument on the roof, you said Lena’s name to stop her.
response: He doesn’t raise his voice. He doesn’t have to. Lena stops as if he had put his hand over her mouth — he hasn’t; he hasn’t moved — and she turns on him with her whole body, the sleeves up, ready to take his head off for it, her mouth already open on *Excuse me* —
And then she sees Margot, and her mouth closes.
Margot, not loud: “This stopped being a game an hour ago.”
Margot doesn’t answer him. She doesn’t look up from the candle.
Lena stops in the middle of a word and looks at Jack, and then at where he’s looking.
Margot, not loud: “This stopped being a game an hour ago.”
He keeps his mouth shut, and Lena finishes. “— and it wasn’t a mother, it was a man in a white coat, with a pamphlet.”

Then the quiet comes in by itself. Nobody stops her; nothing answers her; the HVAC hums. She hears it arrive. Jack watches her hear it — the sleeves, the open hand, the next point dying in her chest — and turn, slowly, to Margot.
Margot, not loud: “This stopped being a game an hour ago.”

s06b.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:05 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE ROOF
body: Margot takes off her glasses. Jack has never seen her without them; her face looks unfinished, younger, the bridge of her nose marked pink where they sit. She folds them and holds them in her lap and says it flat, like a date on a form.
“March of 2000. I was nine. My mother was forty-one. They did an amnio at about sixteen weeks. Trisomy twenty-one.”
Down in the Anacapa lot a car alarm chirps twice and gives up.

“They decided at the kitchen table, and they told me the same night.” She sets the next part off by itself, like a diagnosis. “*In age-appropriate language.* That was my father’s phrase. He was very proud of it.” She turns the glasses over. “It was the fifteenth of March. The ides. My father pointed that out. He thought it was interesting.”
Lena has a hand over her mouth.

“I have defended her in every room I’ve ever been in,” Margot says. “I’m going to defend her in this one.” She looks at Lena now, straight at her, with her naked, unfinished face. “I’m not telling you so you’ll be sorry for him. I’m telling you so you’ll know I’m not doing a bit.”
Lena gets as far as “Margot, I didn’t — ” and Margot lifts one hand off the glasses, an inch, and Lena stops.

“I know you didn’t. You couldn’t have.” There’s no edge on it. “That’s what a statistic is for. Nobody in it has a name.” She looks back down at the candle. “Every March fifteenth I take the day. I don’t go to class. I don’t tell anybody what it’s for. Last year I sat in Laurelhurst Park until it got dark. This year I’ll have a roof.”

Jack sits very still on the end of the towel with the cold of the gravel coming up through his jeans. He has a hundred things he could say and every one of them is an argument, and he can feel all of them in his mouth, ready, and none of them is any use to anybody on this roof. Kevin has moved. Jack didn’t see him do it; he’s on the gravel beside Margot now, his knees up, the thermos left behind against the HVAC box.
The breeze comes over the parapet off the Lagoon, colder now. Jack’s mother was past forty when Rosie came.
Lena takes her hand down. Her voice, when it comes, is wrecked and still entirely hers. “What was his name?”
Margot takes long enough that Jack thinks she isn’t going to answer.
“They’d picked Anders.”
“Anders,” Lena says. Not fast. She says it like a name, and not like a word in an argument.

Beside Margot, Kevin says it too, under his breath, the way people at Mass repeat a name when the priest reads it out in the intentions. Jack only catches it because the HVAC picks that second to cut out.
Margot’s chin moves once. “Nobody’s said that out loud since 2000,” she says, “but me.”

Then they’re both crying. Margot does it without making a sound — the tears simply arrive and go down her face and off her jaw onto the black, and she doesn’t wipe them, and she doesn’t look away. Lena does it with all of New Orleans in it: her shoulders, her breath, a hand flat on her own chest, the sound of a girl at a jazz funeral who knew the man. Her eyeliner goes first, in two dark tracks. She wipes at it with the cuff of the cardigan, and the sleeves are still shoved up past her elbows from when she was winning. Neither of them gives an inch.
“She was right,” Margot says.
“I think she was wrong.” Lena’s voice breaks and she goes on through it. “And I think she loved him. And I don’t know what to do with both.”
Margot puts her glasses back on. “Welcome to my kitchen.”

She reaches past the candle for the pack on the cooler, shakes out one clove, and lights it off the flame in the jar, bending close, her hair falling forward. One per grief. It crackles, and the sweet smoke goes up straight in the cold and then leans off toward the Grove. Lena, who has never yet let a cigarette burn in her presence without confiscating it, watches it go up and lets it burn. Margot smokes it slowly, all the way down, and grinds it out on the gravel, and puts the filter in her own pocket.

Kevin doesn’t say anything else. His hand is flat on the gravel beside Margot’s hip, palm down, close and not touching her. Above them the stars go on over the hills, and the candle burns down another quarter inch in the jar.

choices.key: When Margot told you about Anders, you thanked her for telling you.
response: Margot looks at him. Her face is still wet, and she still doesn’t wipe it. Behind the black frames her eyes have gone red at the rims, which in August he wouldn’t have bet a dollar was possible.
“Don’t make it a thing, Costigan,” she says. It’s already a thing, and she reaches for her cup, and drinks.

journal.title: Margot Lindqvist
journal.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Her mother teaches Classics at Reed. Held a wake for a cigarette on the roof and buried it at sea, for the prose. Had a brother. Her mother was forty-one; the test came back; they’d already picked the name. Anders. March 15, 2000. She’s defended her mother in every room since, and she defended her on the roof. Lena said his name. Doesn’t sleep. My friend.

choices.text: Pray, silently, in the next room: *Anders. Margot. Her mother.*
choices.key: On the roof you prayed for Anders, for Margot, and for her mother, and didn’t say so.
response: He doesn’t close his eyes. He doesn’t move his hands. He talks to the next room the way he always does, like somebody just through the doorway with the radio on.

*Okay. Anders. He’s yours; I’m told I’m allowed to hope that, so I’m hoping it, hard. Margot, who’s been carrying the other end of this by herself since she was nine. Her mother. Her mother too. Her mother at the kitchen table. Lord, have mercy. Christ, have mercy.*
Across the candle, Kevin’s eyes are closed and his lips are moving. Jack watches them a while and can’t make out the language.

s06c.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:51 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE ROOF
body: At ten to four Kevin gets up off the gravel and collects his thermos from beside the HVAC box. “I’ll walk you down,” he says to Margot. Not a question.
Margot stands. She lifts the black peacoat off Laney’s empty lawn chair, shakes it out once, and drops it over Lena’s shoulders.

body.text: Lena reaches up to hand it back. “Keep it,” Margot says, buttoning one button of Jack’s flannel. “I’m wearing a Catholic.”
body.else: Lena reaches up to hand it back. “Keep it,” Margot says. “I’m not cold. I’m Scandinavian.”

body: She steps over the shoebox and goes through the propped door, and Kevin goes after her, the thermos under his arm. Through the gap Jack can see the first landing under its caged bulb. On the landing Kevin puts his hand at the small of Margot’s back — just there, lightly, as if there were a crowd to get her through — and they go round the corner like that.
*Kevin and Margot,* Jack thinks. *Huh.*
The candle in the Mason jar is drowning in its own wax; it gutters, catches, gutters, and holds.

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning.

s07.slug: WEDNESDAY · 4:10 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE ROOF
body: The cold comes up through the gravel first. It comes through the tar under the gravel and the seat of his jeans, a dry cold, the hills’ cold and not the ocean’s, with no wet in it anywhere. The Lagoon lies black and still below the parapet. Over the hills the stars are all still there.

Lena has moved to the elevator housing. She sits with her back to the cinderblock and Margot’s black peacoat around her shoulders over the oatmeal cardigan, the coat’s empty sleeves hanging. She works her boots off, the left and then the right, and stands them up together on the gravel, the two brown Justins, resoled twice, like a pair of altar boys waiting to be told where to go. Then she folds her bare feet under her and sits on them.

Jack sits down against the housing too. The block is cold already, and then colder. Down on the Commons the sprinklers come on, one zone and then the next, a hiss he can just make out from five floors up, and somewhere past the Lagoon the surf on Campus Point keeps up its long, even noise.
She isn’t crying now. Her face is washed clean and quiet in the starlight, and her hair is coming down out of whatever she did to it at sundown, and she is looking at the hills.
“We cry at weddings and wakes,” she says. “That was both.”

choices.text: “You argued that like it was yours.”
response: “You argued that like it was yours,” he says.

It’s her line. She gave it to him across the oak in Hollis 302, low, packing up, and it has been riding around with him ever since. Her hand comes up out of the peacoat to the medal at her throat, the worn gold on its thin chain, and closes on it. “It’s everybody’s, Costigan.” Then she lets go.
“Mine was about my brother,” he says.
“I know,” Lena says. She was there, in the cloister, the afternoon he told her.
“Are you okay?”
“No,” she says, right away, as if she’s been waiting all night for somebody to ask so she could get it over with. “Ask me Thursday.”
He nods. She turns her head against the cinderblock to look at him, to make sure he’s taken it as an appointment and not a dismissal. “I’ll be okay Thursday.”

choices.text: Hand her the last of the pie.

response.text: He reaches over for the Anchor’s box and holds it out: one wedge left in the foil tin, the purple gone nearly black in the cold. Lena eats it with her fingers, straight out of the tin, without apology. “It’s an eight,” she says, and licks her thumb. “It’s a nine.” “It’s an eight at four in the morning.”

He reaches over for the Anchor’s box and holds it out: the last wedge of pecan in the foil, the glaze gone hard in the cold. Lena eats it with her fingers, slowly, the top cracking under her teeth like the sugar on a crème brûlée. He knows what Gloria called her across the counter the Saturday before last; from her face, so does she. She doesn’t say it twice tonight. She finishes it, and licks her thumb.

He reaches over for the Anchor’s box and holds it out. One slice of rhubarb is left in the foil, pink and sour and cold. Lena looks at it. “Margot’s pie,” she says. “Margot’s pie,” Jack says. Neither of them takes it. He sets the box on the gravel at their feet with the lid open, and it sits there the rest of the night like a chaperone.

s07b.slug: WEDNESDAY · 6:20 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE ROOF
body: They talk about the Saints in Buffalo on Sunday, and about whether Augustine was any kind of son to Monica, and about what a po’boy would cost in California if anybody here knew how to make one, and then they don’t talk, and at some point she is asleep against the housing with her chin down in Margot’s collar, and at some point so is he.

At 6:20 he wakes with gravel printed into his left palm and no feeling at all in his left foot. The stars are gone, all but one low over the hills, too steady to be a star. The sky over the ridges has gone from black to a deep cold blue and is getting lighter while he watches, like water getting lighter as you come up through it. A groundskeeper’s cart whines along the path below with its headlights still on. The Grove is giving off its morning eucalyptus, sharp as a cough drop, and the gulls are up.
Lena is awake. She hasn’t moved. She is sitting on her feet with the coat pulled around her, watching the hills come up out of the dark one ridge at a time.
“Yesterday the sun crossed the equator,” she says, when she sees he’s awake. “Twelve and twelve.”
“And now?”
“Now the nights get longer.” She pulls the coat in tighter. “Every day a little, till Christmas.”

Jack thinks of Youngstown at Christmas: dark by five, the snow gone gray by noon, his father’s truck idling in the drive with the heater on high and the left blinker still out. He knows where he’ll be for the longest night of the year. He doesn’t know where she’ll be, and he finds that he would like to.

Her shoulder is near his against the cinderblock, near enough that he can feel the warmth of her through Margot’s wool, and he wants her — not the argument, not the idea of her, her: the weight of her against his side, her head down on his shoulder, her mouth — and he puts both hands flat on the cold gravel and does not move them.
“Sunday, at the tower, Jack,” Lena says. “I didn’t finish a sentence.”

choices.key: On the roof at dawn Lena said she hadn’t finished a sentence. You told her she didn’t have to.
response: “You don’t have to finish it,” he says.
She turns her head on the block and looks at him. The hills go on getting light behind her.
“I’m not going to finish it,” she says. “Not on a roof at six in the morning in Margot’s coat.”
And he lets her.

choices.key: On the roof at dawn Lena said she hadn’t finished a sentence. You told her you’d noticed.
response: “I noticed,” he says.
“I know you did.” She pulls Margot’s collar up to her chin.
“I’m not going to finish it,” she says. “Not on a roof at six in the morning in Margot’s coat.”
And he lets her.

choices.key: On the roof at dawn Lena said she hadn’t finished a sentence. You offered to finish it for her.
response: “I could finish it for you.”
“Don’t you dare, Costigan.” She nearly laughs. She shuts her mouth on it instead and looks at him with her eyes very bright, and for a second the whole roof is too small to hold the two of them.
“I’m not going to finish it,” she says. “Not on a roof at six in the morning in Margot’s coat.”
And he lets her.

choices.key: On the roof at dawn Lena said she hadn’t finished a sentence. You said nothing, and waited.
response: He waits.
So does she. A gull goes over low, complaining. The hills get a shade bluer. Down on the path the groundskeeper’s cart stops, and starts again, and stops.
“I’m not going to finish it,” Lena says finally. “Not on a roof at six in the morning in Margot’s coat.”
And he lets her.

s07c.slug: WEDNESDAY · 6:41 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE ROOF
body: The top of the ridge catches first, one long stretch of it, a line of gold laid along the brush, and then the light starts down the hills toward the town. The Lagoon goes from gray to pewter. Somebody on the third floor opens a window and shuts it again.

“Wes called at eight-oh-four,” Lena says. “Last night. On the dot.” She took it on the east stairs, she says, before she came up. From his room, not from anywhere loud. He sounded tired. “He bought a ticket,” she says. “Columbus Day weekend. He wants to see the Pacific.” She looks at the gold coming down the hills. “I told him it’s a threat.”
Columbus Day weekend is two weeks from Friday. Jack has the arithmetic done before she’s finished saying it.
“You’ll like him,” Lena says. “Everybody does.”

choices.key: When Lena told you Wes is coming for Columbus Day, you said you’d like to meet him.
response: “I’d like to meet him,” Jack says, and means it, which is no help to anybody.
She looks at him, there against the block with the sun finally on her face. “I know you would,” she says. “That’s the worst thing about you.”

At seven Ferrer Tower starts the day’s chimes across the Commons, one bell flat the way it always is, and the sound reaches the roof a little late, off the water. Lena gets up. It lies across the carpet in long bright panels and climbs the side of the Zenith on its cart, and somebody’s Cup Noodles from last night is on the windowsill with the fork still standing in it. Margot’s capitals have been up on the whiteboard since sometime after four.

body: Jack reads it from the doorway. In 412 he lies down on top of the blanket in his clothes, with the gravel still in the seams of his jeans, and sleeps till noon.

Hollis 302 at two minutes to one: the long oak table, the fourteen chairs, the window full of sea. It’s the first full day of fall and it doesn’t look it. The light is high and white, and the Pacific lies flat as hammered tin all the way out to where it stops.

Jack is on two naps’ worth of sleep, in the jeans with the roof still in them and the cleanest shirt he could find, the Augustine in his back pocket. Across the table Lena has on a yellow sundress and the oatmeal cardigan, her hair still wet from the shower and combed straight back, no makeup; nobody did her eyeliner this morning. They haven’t said a word to each other since the chimes.

body.text: Everything in the room is a little too loud: chair legs on the floor, a pen cap at the far end, the light coming off the water like something thrown.
When she sits down she gives him a nod, a seminar nod, the one she gives the Palo Alto girl; and then, when Hale isn’t looking, another one that isn’t.
When she sits down she doesn’t look up at all. She uncaps her pen and reads her own paper as if somebody else wrote it.
When she sits down she gives him a nod, a seminar nod, the one she gives the Palo Alto girl.

body: Caleb has his *Consolations* out, molting Post-its from every edge. Yusuf is drawing small load arrows in the margin of his Lewis. The Palo Alto girl keeps her Montaigne in a Ziploc bag, for reasons she has never shared.

Hale is late, which for Hale is on time. He comes in with the roster and nothing else and sits. “St. Pius of Pietrelcina,” he announces, “whom his own Church investigated for years for bleeding too convincingly. My sort of saint: under suspicion.” “Under suspicion is where they start, Professor,” Lena says, without looking up. “It’s where they end up that’s the scandal.” Hale looks delighted to have been answered. Then his eye travels down the table to the two of them, to Jack’s unshaved jaw and Lena’s wet hair, and something in his ruined handsome face lights like a boy’s at a bonfire. “Mr. Costigan. Miss Broussard. You look like the morning after the Diet of Worms.”

Monday he gave them friendship. Aristotle, the *Ethics*, books eight and nine; Montaigne, “Of Friendship”; Lewis, *The Four Loves*, chapter four, “so the believers at this table have a Christian to hide behind.” One question on the whiteboard, CAN A MAN AND A WOMAN BE FRIENDS?, and the house rule as ever: argue the side you least believe you can prove. Jack wrote his Monday night at the desk in 412 between eleven and two, and read the Lewis chapter through twice, and didn’t ask her which side she was taking. She didn’t ask him.
The papers go across the table at the top of the hour, the way they always do. Hers lands in front of him, two pages stapled at the corner. His is in her hands.
“State your theses,” Hale says.
“That a Man and a Woman Can Be Friends,” Jack says.
“That They Can’t,” says Lena.
The Palo Alto girl looks from one of them to the other. Caleb puts down his pen. “Are we sure,” Caleb says, “this is about Aristotle?”
“Prove the thing you least believe you can prove,” Hale says, with enormous satisfaction. “I see you were both listening.”

Lena goes first. Lena always goes first. “Aristotle,” she says, “wants a friendship between a man and a woman, and he can find only one place to put it. Book eight, chapter twelve: husband and wife. It can be a friendship of virtue, he says, *if they are good* — but it’s in the part about running a household. He shelves us under marriage. Montaigne goes further.” She turns a page of her Montaigne, which is flagged in red. “Women, says Michel de Montaigne, haven’t got souls firm enough to bear the strain of so tight and lasting a knot. I’d like that read into the minutes as the stupidest thing a Frenchman ever wrote” — the table laughs — “and then I’m going to use it. And then there’s Lewis.”
She has the Lewis open, and she reads it aloud, every consonant paid for. “Friendship between a man and a woman *will very easily pass — may pass in the first half-hour — into erotic love.*”
She stops there, and closes the book on her finger. Lewis keeps going after that, as Jack well knows. Nobody in the room reads the rest of it aloud.

choices.text: Aristotle back at her: a friend is another self. You want his good for his sake.
response: “Book nine, chapter four,” Jack says. “A friend is another self. And book eight, chapter three: the friendship of the good wishes the other one’s good *for the other one’s sake*. Not for what it gets. Eros wants to have. A friend wants you to flourish.”
“That’s Aristotle on two men at a gymnasium,” Lena says. “Put a woman in the room.” She’s pleased with him; he can see it in the set of her mouth, and he can see her not liking it.

choices.text: “Then nobody turn their head. I’ve been practicing.”
response: “Then nobody turn their head,” Jack says. “I’ve been practicing.”

The table goes up. The San Diego boys laugh in harmony. Caleb lifts a palm to heaven and says “Selah.” Lena looks at Jack across the oak. “Practicing on whom?” she says, and from her face she’d like it back the second it’s out. Nobody answers.
“Lewis is right about the half-hour,” Jack says.
Somewhere down the table there’s a sound like a dropped fork. Yusuf studies the ceiling. Lena, for once, has no next line ready, and picks up her coffee and drinks some of it instead.
“The gentleman from Ohio concedes the half-hour,” Hale says. “We’ll none of us ask which one.”

choices.text: Augustine, Book Four: the danger is loving somebody mortal as if she’ll never die.
response: He doesn’t need to take the Augustine out of his pocket; he knows the page. “Book Four,” he says. “Augustine has a friend, and loves him as if neither of them would ever die. Then the friend dies. What Augustine is afraid of is loving somebody mortal as if she’ll never die. That’s what wrecks you.”
Hale sits up. “The bishop of Hippo,” he says, “before lunch. Miss Broussard?”
Lena looks at Jack across the table. “Don’t bring Book Four to a seminar,” she says, “unless you mean it.”

body: Half an hour in, Lena breaks her own paper.

“Except,” she says, and sets down her pen, and Jack watches her walk away from two pages she spent Monday night on. “Except Thomas. *Secunda secundae*, question twenty-three, article one. Charity — the highest love there is, the one we’re commanded to — *is* a friendship. Friendship with God. He gets it from John: *I no longer call you servants. I have called you friends.*” Her voice has dropped into the one she uses for the responses at Mass. “If the highest love there is is a friendship, then friendship can’t be the thing eros ruins. It’s the thing eros is *for*.”
Hale sits back, slowly. His horse has come in. “Miss Broussard,” he says, “has just proved Mr. Costigan’s paper.” He turns. “Mr. Costigan — defend hers.”
So Jack has her two pages under his hand and her side to argue, and across the table she has his, and the side she believes. She doesn’t wait for him to find his feet.

He turns over her first page for something to stand on. Aristotle, Montaigne, Lewis, laid down in her order and tamped flat, the whole thing built like a levee. It’s a good paper for a side she doesn’t hold, and now it’s his.
“A friend,” Lena says, “wants your good even when your good is somebody else.”
She says it straight down the oak at him.

choices.text: Aristotle’s best case has a vow in it.
response: “Then explain your own Aristotle,” Jack says. “Book eight, chapter twelve. When the Philosopher goes looking for a friendship of virtue between a man and a woman, the only one he can find has a wedding in it. He couldn’t picture it without the vow. Neither could anybody else for two thousand years.”
“Then the Philosopher,” Lena says, “needed to get out more.” Jack looks down at her pages: she made the same point herself, Monday night, in a footnote. He uses it anyway.

choices.text: “Lewis had already married his friend when he wrote that.”
choices.key: In Hale’s seminar you said C.S. Lewis had already married his friend when he wrote the friendship chapter.
response: “Lewis had already married his friend when he wrote that,” Jack says.

The table looks at him. “Joy Davidman,” he says. “She wrote him letters for years before she ever crossed the ocean. His friend. He married her in a registry office in ’56 so she could stay in England, and then again, properly, at her bedside in a hospital in ’57, when they thought she was dying. He gave the talks the book came out of in ’58. When Lewis says it may pass in the first half-hour, he isn’t guessing.”
Lena goes quiet — the real quiet, not the polite one, and he has only seen it a few times.
“Point to Mr. Costigan,” Hale says softly, “and I believe a casualty.”
Jack looks down at her pages under his hand, and up at her. “Yeah,” he says. “It does.”
He’s supposed to be arguing Can’t. He has just given her Can, outright, in front of the whole table and a man who wrote a bestseller against God.
“Mr. Costigan,” Hale says, “has defected to his own paper.”
Lena turns back a page of his paper she has already read, and reads it again.

choices.text: “Miss Broussard has proved my paper. I wrote it first.”
response: “Miss Broussard has proved my paper,” Jack says. “I wrote it first.”
“Irrelevant,” says Hale.
“Plagiarism of the future,” says Lena. “It’s a Jesuit thing.”

body: By two the assignment has been left somewhere behind them on the table with the coffee cups, and nobody goes back for it. Lena has her elbows on the oak and her hands loose in front of her, and she isn’t reading from anything.
“Augustine,” she says, “grieved his friend for one book and spent the rest of it on a God who couldn’t die on him.”

She says it to the window as much as to the table, to the white glare on the water. The room is quieter than a seminar ought to be. Yusuf has stopped drawing load arrows in his margin. Caleb sits with his hand flat on his *Consolations*. Hale has his chin on his fist and isn’t refereeing anything; he’s listening.
Jack’s own pencil is thickest in that book, in the margins of the chapters where the friend dies.

choices.text: Book Four, chapter nine: you only lose the friends you didn’t love in God.
response: “Chapter nine,” Jack says. He doesn’t take the book out. “*Blessed are those who love you, and love their friends in you.* They’re the only ones who never lose anybody dear to them, he says, because they love them in the one who can’t be lost.” He waits until she looks at him. “He didn’t trade his friend for God, Lena. He found the only place you don’t lose one.”
She has one. “Then why,” she says, “does he spend nine more books making sure he never needs another one?” But she says it to her hands on the oak.

choices.text: “He never got over it. Nobody’s supposed to.”
response: “He never got over it,” Jack says. “Nobody’s supposed to.”
She looks at him. Then she looks down at the table, at a knot in the grain of the oak. “No,” she says. “Nobody is.”
“That,” Jack says, “is a long rebound.”

The room breaks. The San Diego boys lose it; even the Palo Alto girl laughs into her Ziploc bag. “Augustine’s rebound,” Hale says, wiping one eye. “I’m putting it on the final.” And Lena laughs, once, short and out loud, caught off guard, and while it lasts the whole table is warm again.

choices.text: Montaigne wrote the whole essay because his friend died.
response: “Your Frenchman,” Jack says. “Montaigne. He wrote ‘Of Friendship’ about La Boétie, years after La Boétie was dead. *Because it was he, because it was I.*” He taps her pages. “Everybody writes about friendship afterward, Lena. You only get the essay if you had the friend.”
It’s her own Montaigne, turned around on her. She looks for the hole in it, and he watches her look, and she doesn’t come up with one.

journal.title: Designated antagonists
journal.text: Two pages a week, bled on in red. Week two, hers: “That a Broken Statue Is Still Herakles,” with my sentence on page two. Mine: “That God Is the One Who Pays.” She kept it. Then Hale said it out loud: prove the thing you least believe you can prove. Moral luck — mine: “That the Lucky Man Owes Nothing.” Hers: “That There Is Such a Thing as Luck.” Her red on mine: “You don’t believe a word of this. It’s your best paper.” This week, friendship. Mine: “That a Man and a Woman Can Be Friends.” Hers: “That They Can’t.” Caleb asked if we were sure it was about Aristotle. She kept mine.

body: Hale sits back in his chair and looks down the table at the two of them.

body.text: Nobody wins it. Hale has his mouth open to give it to somebody when Lena speaks first, and not to Jack. To the room. “Wes was my brother’s best friend before he was anything to me,” she says. “He’s followed Luc around since he could walk. I’ve seen it go the one way.” She closes her notebook. “I’ve never seen it go back.” Hale doesn’t say anything for a second, and then he does, gently for him. “A draw,” he says, “and a confession. I’ll take both.” Three–one on the season, and a draw, and Jack couldn’t say who won what.

Hale gives it to Jack. “Mr. Costigan,” he says, “on points — both sets.” Four–one on the season. Across the oak Lena is already packing up, and she says it low, for him and nobody else, with her eyes on the zipper of her bag: “You argued my side better than I did. I’ll never forgive you.”

Hale gives it to Jack. “Mr. Costigan,” he says, “on points — both sets.” Four–one on the season. Across the oak Lena is already packing up, and she says it low, for him and nobody else: “You argued my side better than I did. I’ll never forgive you.”

Hale declines to score it. “I’ve had more rigor out of a Christmas cracker,” he says. “Delightful. Bollocks, but delightful.” No decision; three–one on the season, still, and Caleb is still laughing at something from round two.

Hale doesn’t make them wait. “Miss Broussard,” he says, “on points, and on the Frenchman.” Lena takes it with a nod and no flourish. Three–two on the season, and Jack doesn’t mind it the way he ought to.

body: Then Hale folds his hands on the roster and regards the pair of them with deep contentment. “One of you has proved the other’s thesis,” he says. “I’ll leave you to work out which.”
Chairs scrape. The San Diego boys go out arguing about something else entirely. When Jack looks up from her two pages, her chair is pushed back and empty, and his paper is gone with it.
He stands. From the end of the table, without looking up, Hale lifts one finger at him: stay.

Hollis 302 empties fast, and pretends it isn’t. Caleb rounds up his Post-its. Yusuf caps his pen and leaves his load diagrams on the table for somebody else to worry about. The Palo Alto girl is in the hall on her phone before the door has closed. The afternoon lies along the table, the sea in the window gone white with glare, and Lena’s chair stands pushed back at an angle, the way she left it.
Hale stays perched on the table’s end with one long leg swinging. The linen jacket has its wine on the cuff. “How are my margins?” “One.” “One is a beginning.”

body.text: He reaches inside the jacket and comes out with a book the size of a deck of cards. *A Shropshire Lad*, a pocket edition, the paper browned and freckled through — foxed — the cloth worn to the board at the corners, and on the back of the title page, in small capitals, a notice that the book has been produced in complete conformity with the authorized economy standards. Wartime. It was made to go in a pocket and through a war. Hale sets it on the table and moves it across the wood toward Jack with one finger. “For the brother,” he says. “No margins. They’d only erase them.”
body.else: Then he lifts the finger again, toward the door, and lets him go.

body.text: Jack picks it up and it falls open by itself, where it’s been opened before. LIV. *With rue my heart is laden / For golden friends I had.* He knows the rest. Mrs. Pagliarulo made the whole junior class learn it, and two weeks ago, at half past twelve at night in the Anchor’s back booth, he finished it for a drunk man who was saying it to the window. He holds the book open at the page, and in the window the sea goes on being white.

body: Anacapa Commons at half past twelve is a thousand freshmen and one waffle iron. The waffle line goes back past the cereal dispensers; the panini line goes out the door into the sun. Kevin has the corner table by the window, as promised, his tray squared to the edge of it and on the tray a salad that is less a salad than a set of figures: grilled chicken, egg whites, chickpeas, one measured fist of spinach. He’s back in a quarter-zip, Bellarmine maroon, zipped to the collarbone.
Jack sits down with a square of Thursday lasagna and two cookies, grinning before he’s all the way in the chair. He has been grinning about it, on and off, for a day and a half.
“So,” he says. “You and Margot.”

Kevin’s fork stops on its way up, a cube of chicken on the end of it. Behind him somebody drops a tray, and the near half of the Commons applauds, and the fork waits through all of it. Then the big laugh comes, the team-captain laugh that fills a table, and the chicken goes where it was going.
“Margot and me,” Kevin says. “Sure. Let’s go with that.” He points the empty fork across the table. “Respectfully, bro, she’d dissect me. For science.”

He’s seen the wall post — all of Delgado has seen the wall post, both exclamation points — and he wants to know where she’s taking him Friday. “She won’t say.” “That tracks. She ran the cleanup like a cattle drive.” Does Jack own anything warm? Kevin listens to every answer with his chin on his fist, sunny and interested, as if Friday were the only news on the board.

Kevin’s laugh lands right on cue. “Tell Theo,” he says, “and I tell Becca you can’t tell a heifer from a steer.” “I can tell a heifer from a steer.” “Can you, though? On a Friday night? With the lights off?” He takes one of Jack’s cookies as a fine, and Jack lets him have it.

Jack lets it go and asks about the quiz instead, and Kevin gives him three minutes on chirality with the salt and pepper shakers: two molecules built of the same parts, mirror images, that won’t lie down on top of each other however you turn them. Gregory came through.” At the tray return, sliding his tray onto the belt, Kevin says, “Thanks, man,” and is gone toward the Chem building at a jog before Jack can work out what for.

s09b.slug: THURSDAY · 12:30 PM · THE UCEN, THE TIDE NEWSROOM
body: The *Marisol Tide* lives up a flight of stairs from the Panda Express, in a long room that smells of orange chicken and toner and has never been aired out. Back issues stand along the walls in twine-tied bundles, a geological history of student outrage. On the desk by the window a dead iMac G4 — the white dome, the lamp-arm neck — has been put to work holding up the AP Stylebook, and beside it a living one hums under Margot’s hands. She is the only person in the room. “Sit,” she says, typing.

His flannel is on top of the dead iMac, folded in a square as tight as a flag at a Youngstown funeral. “It’s been washed,” Margot says. “Don’t read into it.”

I need one quote from an actual believer so they can’t say I made you up.” She turns the chair to face him. “What does your Church do that’s a story and not a scandal?”

The cursor blinks while he thinks. “Somebody sits with the dying,” he says. “Every parish. Every night of the week, somebody’s in a hospital chair next to somebody nobody else is coming to see. Nobody’s ever written it up. It hasn’t got a villain.”
Margot turns back and types it, all of it, in his order, without comment, and hits save.

body: “Kierkegaard divides love in two,” Evan says. He never writes on the board. “Preferential love — the beloved, the friend, the ones you choose. And love of the neighbor, which you don’t get to choose, because the neighbor is whoever’s there.” He turns a page. “Kierkegaard thought the beloved and the friend were the self loved twice. Only the neighbor is the other.”
Lena’s pen comes up. “Then he never had a friend.”

Evan considers that. “He was engaged once,” he says. “Regine Olsen. He gave back the ring and wrote about her for the rest of his life.” He takes off his wire glasses, rubs the two red marks they’ve worn into the bridge of his nose, and puts them back on.

At ten to five Evan lets them go. Jack passes her paper across the aisle — “That They Can’t,” his red all through it from Wednesday night. She turns to page two first. She always does. His own paper doesn’t come back the other way.
“I’m not done with yours,” she says.

“Sunday.”

response: At the bottom of page two, beside her best paragraph, in his red: *Cite me.* Her own margin word, in his handwriting. She laughs once, through her nose, and doesn’t cross it out.

s10.slug: FRIDAY · 5:59 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL
body: At a minute to six on Friday the Fishbowl is full of people who just happen to be there. Laney is on the long couch in her Pi Lam letters, pink on white, her feet tucked under her, doing nothing with tremendous concentration. Lena is on the arm of the same couch with a Hansen and Quinn open on her knee, because Laney dragged her down for what Laney called a study break, and she has been on the same page of the aorist since she sat. Theo is at the broken foosball table with the MacBook balanced across the goalie rods, editing something with the sound off. Kevin and Doug Pruitt have the far couch under the TV, where the President, on tape from the morning, is at a podium in Pittsburgh talking about a secret plant in Iran, and Doug wants to know if Qom is near Bakersfield, because it sounds near Bakersfield.

Jack comes down in the Carhartt jacket, too big in the shoulders, because the wall post said to dress warm. At 5:59 a red pickup with Idaho plates turns into the circle out front and stops square in the fire lane, and Becca Lindell comes through both sets of doors at a ranch walk: Ropers, Wranglers, the Carhartt vest, the braid, the keys swinging off the steel carabiner on one finger. “I’m early,” she says, to everybody. “I’m always early. It’s a ranch thing.”
“Is she Amish,” Laney says, at a volume built for pageant stages, “or just punctual?”
Lena closes the grammar on one finger. “Laney. Be nice.” She means it. It’s in the finger, holding her place.
“I *am* nice,” says Laney. “I’m being *accurate*.”

Theo has already risen from the foosball table and crossed the room with his hand out, as if he’s been waiting his whole life to be introduced. “Becca. Theo Vance.” The handshake is perfect: warm, brief, a little reverent. “I’ve heard you can butcher a deer.”
Becca lights up like he’s asked after her family. “Elk too.”

Theo receives this in reverent silence, and goes back to the foosball table, and his thumbs go to work on the iPhone below the edge of it. Across the room, on the couch cushion, Laney’s pink BlackBerry buzzes. She reads it. She looks at Theo. Theo looks at the foosball men on their rods, at the middle distance, at nothing.
Kevin doesn’t look away from the TV. “Leave it alone,” he says.

body.text: Lena, from the arm of the couch, to Becca: “Have fun. If he tries to explain football to you — ”
body.else: Lena, from the arm of the couch, to Becca: “Have fun.” The finger goes back into the grammar.

body.text: “Oh, he’ll get his chance,” Becca says, beaming at her, and at Jack, and at the whole Fishbowl, which she seems to find lovely. “It’s football! Marisol High, under the lights. I’ve got a blanket in the truck.”

response: Laney blows him a kiss off the flat of her palm, full pageant. “*Never*, fireman.” The BlackBerry is buzzing again before the kiss has crossed the room.

Becca holds the Fishbowl door for him, and they go out across the lobby, and behind them the whole Fishbowl turns on its couches to watch through the glass — Laney, Theo, Kevin, Doug, the President of the United States — as if the lobby had come on TV.

Lena opens the grammar again to the page her finger was keeping. “I never do, Costigan.” She turns the page. Her composure is flawless. On the couch below her, Laney’s eyebrows have gone up into the copper hair and taken up residence.

s10b.slug: FRIDAY · 7:05 PM · MARISOL HIGH SCHOOL, MARINER FIELD
body: The Ranger is a ’94, red where it isn’t primer, with a feed-store sticker from Rathdrum on the back glass, and inside it smells like hay and old coffee and every pickup in Youngstown. Clipped to the driver’s visor is a St. Isidore the Farmer medal, the saint walking behind his plow. Becca drives with one hand at twelve o’clock and the other out the window, down Mission and up the hill, talking about Eli’s clutch like it’s a family member with a temper.

At the card table by the gate it’s five dollars a head, and Jack has his wallet out and Becca has already paid. “I asked, I pay,” she says. “Next time you can.” She buys the hot dogs too, and two cans of pop, and takes a stadium blanket out of the truck bed, red plaid, smelling of truck bed.

Mariner Field is every high-school field in America, which is the whole pleasure of it: the lights coming on against a sky still pink over the hills, a band in wool coats too hot for September, cut grass and kettle corn. The Marisol High Mariners against the Arroyo Seco Broncs, who came over the hills on two yellow buses and yell like four. Becca knows downs. She knows them the way Frank knows them, from the inside, and by the end of the first quarter she has explained a zone blitz to the grandfather in front of them and stood up twice to tell the referee about a hold he didn’t call.

Late in the second quarter the Mariners line up on fourth and one at the Broncs’ thirty-eight. Becca puts her hot dog down on the blanket, shuts her eyes, and says the Glory Be out loud, fast, all of it in the time it takes the quarterback to get under center — *as it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be* — and the quarterback sneaks it, and the pile leans, and the chains come out, and it’s a first down by the width of a hand. She opens her eyes. “See?” she says. “It’s short on purpose.”

The Mariners’ mascot is a man in a sea captain’s coat and a foam peg leg who stumps up and down the track in front of the student section with a harpoon made of a pool noodle, and the student section calls him Ahab and chants it every time the Broncs have the ball. And Jack has the joke already built — the leg, the whale, which of the two teams is the whale, the whole timing of it down to the pause before the last line — and it’s built for someone who isn’t on these bleachers. He holds it. Then he puts it away, and eats his hot dog.

At halftime the PA comes on with Miley Cyrus, and the whole student section gets up on the benches to sing it, and so does Becca, who knows every word and doesn’t care in the slightest who sees her know them. She sits down pink and pleased. “I have two sisters,” she says, which explains it.
Then she turns to him on the blanket. “Teach me one of the proofs. The first one. The ones with numbers.” “The Five Ways.” “The first one.”

So he teaches her the First Way, on the home bleachers at Mariner Field, with mustard on his thumb. Things move — not just across a floor; they change, they go from could-be to is. A cold pan gets hot. But nothing gets itself from could-be to is; something already hot has to heat it. Line them up, the pan, the burner, the gas, and you can’t go back forever, because with no first there’s no second and no hot pan, and there’s the pan, hot. So there’s a first mover that nothing moved. “And this everyone understands to be God,” he says. “That’s Aquinas. That’s the end of it.”

Becca says it back perfectly. She does it with a newborn calf in a cold barn, a heat lamp, a generator, a diesel truck and her father, and doesn’t drop a step, and lands on *God* with both feet. “That’s good,” she says. “That’s *so* good.” She hugs her knees inside the blanket and looks at the empty field, happy.

“Do you ever think it might not be true?” she asks, as easily as asking whether he takes cream. Then, before he can answer: “I don’t. I’ve never once.” She turns and looks at him, honestly puzzled, the braid over one shoulder, sunburn along her part under the stadium lights. “Do you?”

choices.text: “Not whether it’s true. Whether I’m any good at it. At two in the morning.”
choices.key: On the bleachers Becca asked if you ever think it might not be true. You said not whether it’s true: whether you’re any good at it, at two in the morning.
response: She thinks about that with her whole face — eyebrows, mouth, freckles — as if it were a calf turned wrong. Then it clears. “Then I’ll pray for two in the morning,” she says, and picks her hot dog back up, and he believes her: every night, on the rosary, wherever it is she sleeps, with the lights out.
“Good,” Becca says, and pats his knee through the blanket: settled. The band comes back up the stairs. The teams come out of the field house. The third quarter starts as though nobody asked anything.

Becca laughs, a big ranch-kitchen laugh that turns the grandfather around in his seat. Then she folds her hands on the blanket, very serious, and adds the Cleveland Browns to her prayer list out loud, between Eli’s clutch and her mother’s bad knee.

s10c.slug: FRIDAY · 9:40 PM · PORTOLÁ HALL, THE PARKING LOT
body: The Mariners won it by a field goal with a minute to go, and Becca honked the Ranger’s horn twice at every light on Mission, for the team. Now the truck sits under the sodium light in the Portolá lot with the engine ticking as it cools. The cab has gone quiet. St. Isidore turns a little on his clip. Becca has the keys in her lap on the carabiner, and across the lot, through the eucalyptus, Delgado is lit up in its grid.

“That was a good game,” she says. He agrees, and it was. Then she leans across the bench seat, quick and certain, and kisses him on the cheek, high up, where the stubble starts, and sits back behind the wheel.
“So there’s no confusion,” she says.

response: She nods once, satisfied, like a gate latched. “Good night, Jack.” She goes up the walk to Portolá swinging the keys, and at the door she turns and waves with her whole arm, the pasture wave, until he waves back.
He leans across and kisses her cheek back. Sunburn and hay and Ivory soap. She laughs, pleased, gone pink all the way to the braid. “Okay then,” she says, and gets out of the truck still laughing.

She waits, the keys quiet in her lap. He doesn’t have the rest of it. She waits some more, kindly, with all the time in the world, and then she smiles at him under the sodium light. “Next Friday?” she says. “I’ll ask again Tuesday.”

s11.slug: SATURDAY · 12:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, EAST STAIRWELL, 4TH-FLOOR LANDING
body: At twenty to one on a Saturday the east stairwell is warm. The sun has been on the landing window since eleven and the concrete has drunk it, and the window is open its six inches on a Lagoon so blue it looks retouched. Jack sits on the top step with his back to the wall. The RAZR is wedged into the top corner of the frame, where the one good bar lives. Ohio State beat Illinois this morning while he watched the second half on Theo’s MacBook with Theo asleep beside it: a shutout, and Theo woke up long enough to ask who Pryor was.

Twenty to four on Glenwood Avenue. His mother picks up with the TV going behind her and starts in the middle. Pittsburgh has been on the news all week, she tells him, the G-20, every president in the world, protesters with bandanas over their faces and the bridges shut down, sixty-some miles away and you’d think it was the moon. Then, quick, tucked in between the bridges and the next thing: his father has a meeting at the union hall Tuesday. Then the next thing. “Nonna’s card came yesterday. From your priest. She put it on the refrigerator next to Rosie’s spelling test, Jackie. She made Mrs. Iannucci come in and look at it.”
A click, the extension in the front room, and the post-game show comes in behind it. “Thirty-nothing,” his father says. “Shutout.” “I saw.” “Good.” Click.
Then his mother, in a different voice, the one she uses at the school office for parents who are behind on tuition: “Who’s Idaho?”

choices.text: “Her name’s Becca. Seven brothers and sisters. A ranch.”
response: “*Seven!*” His mother says it the way other people say *jackpot*. “Catholic?” “Very.” A kitchen chair scrapes. Somewhere behind her, from the direction of the stairs, Gina, at full volume: “*SHE DRIVES.*”
“A girl from church,” his mother repeats, in a tone that forgets nothing. “Gina says she drives.”
“Idaho is *somebody*,” his mother says. “Gina showed me her picture on the computer. She looks like a nice girl.” Then a pause with *you never tell me anything* in it.
