Lena is in a black WHO DAT shirt with a gold ribbon through her hair, and at Sully’s she slides into the booth under the big screen, takes one look at Jack’s black T-shirt, digs in her tote, and lobs a string of gold Mardi Gras beads across the table at him. “There,” she says. “Now you’re dressed.” At the end of the bar Dale Wisniewski, in the Barry Sanders jersey, doesn’t turn around. “The loud one,” he tells the little set over the register, which has the Lions on it, at home to the Redskins, and which he hasn’t taken his eyes off since kickoff.

It’s an ugly game, gray and grinding up in Buffalo. Brees can’t find anybody, and in the fourth quarter Dale reads his line off the crawl and shakes his head at it — sixteen of twenty-nine, a hundred seventy-two yards, no touchdowns. Lena could not care less. She’s in love with the defense. Every time a Bills receiver goes down short of the sticks she’s on her feet, and every time Pierre Thomas lowers his head and runs into the middle of Buffalo she shouts, “Go to *work*, baby,” and Kevin pulls the 49ers cap down over his eyes. “Lord have mercy, this is ugly,” she says, radiant. “I love it so much.”

On the tube TV in the corner the Browns are in Baltimore, and it’s worse than ugly. By the fourth quarter it’s thirty-four to three. “Three points,” Jack says. “*Three*.” Nobody at the bar has sympathy to spare for him. Detroit hasn’t won a football game since December of 2007, nineteen straight, and late in the fourth the Lions are ahead, and Dale is off his stool with one hand flat on the bar and his coffee going cold. When the clock runs out at Ford Field, nineteen to fourteen, he doesn’t make a sound. He sits back down and puts both hands over his face and keeps them there. Then he takes them away and finds Jack down the bar, Michigan to Ohio. “It ends,” Dale says. “I’m telling you. It ends.”

body: Lena sees the screen as he tips it to the light. “Then go eat it, dish man,” she says, and turns back to the game. Jack stays put. There’s a game on.

Twenty-seven to seven. On the last whistle Lena is out of the booth and up on the rail before the owner can get there, and she rings Sully’s brass bell herself, with her whole shoulder, and then once more, pointing down the bar at Dale, till the Packers table applauds. In the Anacapa lot after, she wipes the 2–0 off the Odyssey’s back glass with one of Kevin’s gym socks from the back seat, over Kevin’s objections, and writes it big in the white La Vang polish: 3–0. Jack holds the bottle for her and gets it on the heel of his hand.

At nine that night, the college Mass: candles, three guitars, the hull going up into the dark. Numbers: Eldad and Medad prophesying in the camp without anybody’s permission, and Joshua wanting them stopped, and Moses: *Would that all the people of the Lord were prophets!* James, on the wages withheld from the workers, crying out. Then Mark, and the hard part. *If your hand causes you to sin, cut it off.*

Osei preaches without notes, from the step. “Eldad and Medad were not on the list,” he says. “The Spirit does not check the guest list. People hear the knife. I was a doctor; I hear the hand. It is yours. It does what you tell it. That is the frightening part.” He sits.
Jack’s right hand is on his knee. He leaves it there.

At the sign of peace he turns, and in the last pew, in black, with a reporter’s notebook closed on her knee, is Margot Lindqvist. “For the *Tide*,” she says, before he can ask. By Communion the last pew is empty.

The 9:30 is babies and the people who were up with them, sunburned fathers, a row of Vietnamese grandmothers in cardigans, the blue glass bright with morning. The organist, a big gray man with a foghorn voice, leans into the opening hymn. Becca is beside Jack in a clean Carhartt vest over a church blouse, her rosary in her fist, singing all four verses without the book.

Jack’s right hand is on his knee. He leaves it there.

Afterward the courtyard fills up around the folding tables under the olive tree, and the sprinkler hisses at the hedge. Becca is behind Coffee & Donuts in a hospitality apron with ST. BRENDAN’S ironed onto it, and she knows everybody’s order before they reach the front: decaf for the old man with the cane, two sugars for the grandmother in the lavender cardigan, one glazed cut in half for twins who can’t be trusted with a whole. Mrs. Fitch takes her coffee to a folding chair and watches the two of them over the rim.

Tyler Brandt finds Jack by the urns and fist-bumps him without asking. “Brother. You stood me up Wednesday.” “I was asleep. You said Wednesday. You didn’t say when.” “I prayed harder.” Tyler nods across at the table — the braid, the apron, the line moving like a clock — and lowers his voice to something like reverence. “Becca Lindell, brother. That’s a woman with a plan.”

By eleven Mrs. Fitch has said “you two” twice, and one of the Coffee & Donuts ladies has said it once, in the tone of settled business. The maple bar is waiting for him on a napkin with JACK on it in marker, in Becca’s poster lettering. “I said I would,” Becca says, and hands it over, and watches him take the first bite.
